title: Entra Agent ID: blueprints, identities and agent users
summary: Entra Agent ID models an agent as a blueprint that holds credentials, agent identities that carry no credentials, and an optional agent user account. Sponsors and owners give each agent a named accountable human.
useIf: You need to understand what an agent is in Entra, who owns it, and how credentials and lifecycle are controlled.
avoidIf: You only call a model from an app and do not yet need a distinct identity for the agent.

explain.md: Entra Agent ID has four objects: an **agent identity blueprint**, a **blueprint principal**, an **agent identity** and an optional **agent user** [[r17]]. The **agent identity** is a service principal with `servicePrincipalType` `ServiceIdentity` and `@odata.type` `#microsoft.graph.agentIdentity`, and it has **no credentials** [[r17]]. The **blueprint** holds the credentials (federated identity credentials, certificates or keys, or client secrets) and requests tokens for the identities it creates. It is a credential boundary and can federate to an Azure managed identity [[r17]]. Agent identities are single tenant, while blueprints can be multitenant [[r17]].

explain.title: Object model
explain.alt: A blueprint holds credentials and has a blueprint principal. It creates agent identities. Each agent identity may have one optional agent user account.
explain.src:
flowchart TB
  BP[Blueprint: holds credentials] --> BPP[Blueprint principal]
  BP --> AI1[Agent identity A]
  BP --> AI2[Agent identity B]
  AI1 --> AU1[Agent user, optional]

explain.md: The **agent user** is an optional second account: a user object marked as an AI agent, 1:1 with its agent identity. It can hold licenses, a mailbox and OneDrive and be reached through Teams, Outlook and Word comments. It is available only to tenants in the **Frontier preview program** [[r17]]. Foundry provisions a blueprint and identity automatically; in the agent application model unpublished agents share a project identity and publishing creates a dedicated one [[r27]].

explain.title: Blast radius and governance
explain.md: Because the blueprint holds the credentials for every identity it creates, group only identities that can share credentials and a baseline of permissions [[r17]]. Agents have **no MFA**, so Conditional Access (evaluated when a token is issued or refreshed, plus Continuous Access Evaluation for some resources) is the control. It needs Microsoft 365 E7 or an Agent 365 license with at least Entra P1 or Microsoft 365 E3. Entra Agent ID itself is available to all Entra customers [[r15]]. Role-assignable groups and assigned security groups cannot be sponsors [[r18]].

whereToUse: Giving each agent a distinct identity so access, logs and incidents trace to one agent
Setting sponsors and owners so every agent has a named human accountable for it
Applying Conditional Access and ID Governance access packages to agents instead of shared secrets
Deciding whether an agent needs a user account, for mailbox, Teams presence or licenses

use: Use a separate agent identity per agent instance so permissions and audit stay scoped
Use sponsors for business accountability and owners for technical control
Add an agent user only when the agent must act as a team member in Microsoft 365
avoid: Do not put identities with different sensitivity under one blueprint, since credentials are shared at the blueprint
Do not use groups as sponsors that Entra disallows, or as owners
Do not plan on agent users in tenants outside Frontier preview
flips: Agent needs a mailbox or Teams presence: add an agent user (Frontier preview)
Different permission tiers: split blueprints by tier
Credentials must not be stored: federate the blueprint to an Azure managed identity

pitfalls.symptom: Auditors cannot tell which agent called a service
pitfalls.cause: Several agents run under one shared app registration or the project identity
pitfalls.fix: Give each agent its own agent identity and log by identity [[r27]].

pitfalls.symptom: A disabled agent cannot be turned back on by its business owner
pitfalls.cause: Sponsors can disable or soft-delete but cannot re-enable or edit auth settings
pitfalls.fix: Assign an owner (user or service principal) who can re-enable [[r18]].

pitfalls.symptom: Creating a sponsor with a group fails
pitfalls.cause: Role-assignable groups and assigned security groups cannot be sponsors
pitfalls.fix: Use users, or an allowed group type [[r18]].

scenarios.title: One sensitive agent among many routine ones
scenarios.situation: A platform team will register forty agents. Thirty-nine are low risk. One can read confidential records.
constraints: Blueprints hold the credentials of all their identities
unknowns: Do the routine agents share a baseline of permissions?
scenarios.question: How do you structure blueprints?

options.name: A blueprint for the routine group and a separate blueprint for the sensitive agent
options.why: A compromise of one blueprint's credentials then does not expose the sensitive agent, and routine agents still share a baseline.
options.tradeoff: Two credential sets to rotate and monitor.

options.name: One blueprint for all forty
options.why: The blueprint holds credentials for every identity it creates, so one compromise reaches the sensitive agent.
options.tradeoff: Right when all agents share trust level and permissions.

options.name: One blueprint per agent
options.tradeoff: Forty credential sets and heavy operations.

flips.then: One blueprint with strict federation and monitoring.

flips.if: Each agent belongs to a different team

scenarios.takeaway: Group by shared credentials and baseline permissions, not by convenience.

scenarios.title: Who answers for the agent
scenarios.situation: A business unit launches an agent. The product manager wants to be accountable, and a platform engineer manages credentials.
constraints: Every agent needs a named human
Technical rotation is an engineering task
unknowns: Will the PM change roles soon?
Is there a service principal for automation?
scenarios.question: How do you assign sponsors and owners?

options.name: Sponsor: the product manager (user). Owner: the platform engineer (user or service principal)
options.why: Sponsors decide lifecycle and can disable. Owners manage credentials and can re-enable or hard-delete.
options.tradeoff: Two people to keep current when staff change.

options.name: Sponsor: a role-assignable group
options.tradeoff: Some other group types may be allowed, so check type first.

options.name: Sponsor only, no owner
options.why: Meets the minimum of one sponsor.
options.tradeoff: No technical owner to manage credentials or re-enable after a disable.

flips.then: Reassign a sponsor immediately, since at least one is required.
Owner duties shrink, but keep one for re-enable and delete.

scenarios.takeaway: Sponsors carry accountability, owners carry control.

quiz.q: Match each Entra Agent ID object to its role.

pairs.r: Optional user object for mailbox and licenses
Required business accountability, no auth edits

quiz.explain: The blueprint is the credential boundary. The agent identity is a credential-less service principal. The agent user is optional and Frontier-only. Sponsors are required but cannot edit authentication settings.

quiz.q: Why group only similar agents under one blueprint?
options: Blueprints limit the number of tokens
Agent identities cannot be multitenant otherwise
The blueprint holds credentials for every identity it creates
quiz.explain: A compromised blueprint exposes all its identities. Agents have no MFA, and identities are single tenant regardless of blueprint choice.

quiz.q: Which statements about owners and sponsors are supported by the docs?
options: Sponsors are required, at least one per blueprint and agent identity
quiz.explain: Sponsors are required and owners are optional technical admins who can re-enable or hard-delete. Owners are users or service principals, never groups, and sponsors cannot edit auth settings.

flashcards.front: Where do an agent's credentials live in Entra Agent ID?
flashcards.back: On the blueprint, not on the agent identity. The identity is a service principal of type ServiceIdentity with no credentials.
Sponsor: required business accountability, can disable or soft-delete. Owner: optional technical admin (user or service principal), manages credentials and can re-enable or hard-delete.
Agents have no MFA. Conditional Access is evaluated at token issuance or refresh, with Continuous Access Evaluation for some resources.
